newsitem.title: UK: Blair aims to be UK's education prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Blair aims to be UK's education prime minister.

text.p: Tony Blair, hot favourite to be Britain's next prime minister, will rally his Labour party on Tuesday for the coming general election with a promise that education will be his overriding priority.
Aides said Blair would use his keynote speech to the party's annual conference to reinforce his claim to speak for the "radical centre" and mainstream majority in British politics.

Labour, out of power since 1979, leads the ruling Conservatives in polls by more than 20 points and Blair aims to cement that lead by convincing voters that he, rather than Prime Minister John Major, is in touch with their aspirations.
Major, whose party has won four consecutive terms of office, must call a general election by May at the latest.
Blair will promise to "unleash the potential of all the British people" by setting three priorities -- education, education and education, aides say.

Arguing that Britain is falling behind its global economic rivals, Blair will set Labour the goal of turning Britain into a "skills superpower" to compete in the knowledge race that he says has replaced the arms race of the Cold War.

Since he became leader in July 1994, Blair has sought to soothe Labour traditionalists uneasy about his rush to dump leftwing ideals while promising disenchanted Conservatives that he would not reverse all the free-market reforms of the last 17 years.
The run-up to the conference has been overshadowed by speculation that Blair would like to weaken further Labour's links with Britain's trade unions, which founded the party almost a century ago.

Although Blair will signal that he has no such plans, he intends to keep his distance from the unions by describing Labour as "the political arm of the British people" and not the voice just of the labour movement.
The Financial Times said Blair, eager to woo business, would also put the European Union at the centre of his general election campaign.
He is expected to pledge that a Labour government would set a deadline of mid-1998 for the completion of the European Union's single market.
Blair's main task is to woo wavering voters who may be fed up with nearly two decades of Conservative rule but are unsure whether it is "safe" to trust Labour.

Economics spokesman Gordon Brown, on the first day of the conference, sought to provide that reassurance on Monday by warning delegates that there could be no return to discredited tax-and-spend policies.
He offered instead an "iron discipline" on public spending, tempered only by the long-term promise of a "people's tax cut" to lower the starting rate of income tax to 10-15 percent from 24 percent.
